studies.Reference: Fibre intake and prostate cancer risk.
studies.Authors: Pelucchi C, Talamini R, Galeone C, Negri E, Franceschi S, Dal Maso L, Montella M, Conti E, La Vecchia C

sample_size.excerpt: A multicentre case-control study was conducted in Italy from 1991 to 2002, including 1,294 men with incident, histologically confirmed prostate cancer and 1,451 controls admitted to the same network of hospitals as cases with acute nonmalignant conditions.
sample_size.location: Abstract, third sentence; total_n derived from reported group counts 1294 + 1451 = 2745

cases.excerpt: A multicentre case-control study was conducted in Italy from 1991 to 2002, including 1,294 men with incident, histologically confirmed prostate cancer and 1,451 controls admitted to the same network of hospitals as cases with acute nonmalignant conditions.

effect_size.excerpt: Compared to the lowest quintile, the OR of prostate cancer for the highest quintile of total fibre intake was 0.93 (95% CI 0.71-1.22). The risk was inversely related with soluble fibre (OR = 0.89, 95% CI 0.78-1.02, for a difference between 80th and 20th percentile), cellulose (OR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.78-1.01) and vegetable fibre (OR = 0.82, 95% CI 0.73-0.93).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Compared to the lowest quintile, the OR of prostate cancer for the highest quintile of total fibre intake was 0.93 (95% CI 0.71-1.22).

design.excerpt: A multicentre case-control study was conducted in Italy

studies.Reference: Fiber intake and risk of subsequent prostate cancer in Japanese men.
studies.Authors: Sawada N, Iwasaki M, Yamaji T, Shimazu T, Sasazuki S, Inoue M, Tsugane S, Japan Public Health Center–based Prospective Study Group
studies.Journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Participants responded to a validated questionnaire, which included 138 food items.

sample_size.excerpt: We conducted a population-based prospective study in 43,435 Japanese men aged 45-74 y. Participants responded to a validated questionnaire, which included 138 food items.

cases.excerpt: During the 11.6-y follow-up, of the 825 men newly diagnosed with prostate cancer, 213 had advanced-stage cancer, 582 had organ-localized disease, and 30 had an undetermined stage of disease.

effect_size.excerpt: Total fiber was not associated with total or advanced prostate cancer, with respective multivariable HRs for the highest and lowest quartiles of 1.00 (95% CI: 0.77, 1.29; P-trend = 0.97) and 0.67 (95% CI: 0.42, 1.07; P-trend = 0.30). Total fiber and insoluble fiber intake were associated with a decreased risk of advanced cancers detected by subjective symptoms, with multivariate HRs (95% CIs) across increasing quartiles of 1.00, 0.58, 0.62, and 0.44 (0.21, 0.92; P-trend = 0.05) for total fiber and 1.00, 0.60, 0.52, and 0.46 (0.22, 0.93; P-trend = 0.04) for insoluble fiber.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Total fiber was not associated with total or advanced prostate cancer, with respective multivariable HRs for the highest and lowest quartiles of 1.00 (95% CI: 0.77, 1.29; P-trend = 0.97) and 0.67 (95% CI: 0.42, 1.07; P-trend = 0.30).

sample_size.excerpt: A total of 54,336 participants in the United States, consisting of 6,414 patients with PCa, were included in this study.

cases.excerpt: Therefore, this study examined the relationship between fiber intake and the risk of PCa by using data from Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial. A total of 54,336 participants in the United States, consisting of 6,414 patients with PCa, were included in this study.

effect_size.excerpt: Compared with individuals in the lowest quartile, individuals in the highest quartile of insoluble fiber intake had a significantly lower risk of PCa (aHR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.78-0.98). By contrast, no significant associations were detected between total fiber intake (aHR, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.80-1.01) or soluble fiber intake (aHR, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.80-1.02).

extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: lowest quintile=0.84, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.76–0.93), advanced restricted PC (MVHR=0.85, 95%CI 0.74–0.97), and PC mortality (MVHR=0.78, 95%CI 0.68–0.89); statistically significant trends were noted for each of these associations (p≤0.03), while a null association was observed for high grade PC for the same comparison (MVHR=1.00, 95%CI 0.93–1.07).
extraction_supporting_text.design: Pooled analysis of the primary data in 15 cohorts in three continents.
extraction_supporting_text.timing: 842,149 men were followed for up to 9–22 years between 1985–2009 across studies.
extraction_supporting_text.continent: These analyses were conducted using data from 15 cohort studies from North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 7 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.92 (95% CI: 0.86–1.0), suggesting that total dietary fiber intake is associated with a lower risk of prostate cancer. These findings were supported by moderate between-study heterogeneity (I² = 42.94%), suggesting some variability in the results across studies.
